newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein press Britain on IRA prisoner release.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein press Britain on IRA prisoner release.

text.p: Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army, pressed Britain on Monday to free or transfer hundreds of IRA prisoners in its first talks with British officials since the guerrillas declared a new ceasefire a week ago.
Sinn Fein Vice-President Pat Doherty said his team raised the issues when it met London government officials at the final session of multi-party peace talks before a summer adjournment.

He said his party, which shares the IRA's goal of an end to British rule of Northern Ireland, would be meeting Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, for the first time on either Monday or Wednesday of next week.

Mowlam has pledged to review the cases of 30-odd prisoners held in jails on the British mainland for security offences and to look favourably on their transfer to Irish and Northern Irish prisons where hundreds more are serving their sentences.

Doherty's delegation was present at what is expected to be the last session of the slow-moving talks until they resume in September to begin ironing out a lasting settlement to a 28-year conflict that has killed 3,200.
Sinn Fein will be allowed to take part in the negotiations on September 15 if the IRA truce is declared genuine by Britain. Until then the party can only attend bilateral talks with other parties.

Doherty urged the remaining pro-British Protestant party at the talks, David Trimble's Ulster Unionist Party, to shelve objections to rules on the surrender of guerrilla arms and to join the negotiations.
"We want to see the unionists there. If they are not, the door should be left ajar for them, but we should proceed anyway," he said.

The UUP joined two smaller unionist parties in voting down Anglo-Irish proposals that the IRA and pro-British loyalist extremists surrender weapons as the talks progress, rather than before or afterwards.
But it stayed at the talks when the Democratic Unionist Party and UK Unionist Party walked out last week in protest at what they called an appeasement of IRA terrorism.

Government officials fear the UUP will not negotiate directly with Sinn Fein until the IRA is forced to physically surrender some arms during the negotiations, something the guerrillas staunchly refuse to do.
Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams said in a weekend television interview: "There's no possibility -- and the IRA have made this very clear -- of them surrendering their weapons."

There have been no IRA attacks since the truce was proclaimed although British security forces and the 12,000-strong Northern Ireland police remain on the alert against violence by Irish Catholic republicans or their Protestant pro-British loyalist foes.

Police said they had not ruled out sectarianism as a motive for the weekend killing of 16-year-old Catholic youth James Morgan. His body was found in a field near the village of Clough 25 miles (80 km) south of Belfast.

Sinn Fein area councillors said in a statement: "All of the evidence at this time, including the arrest of several very prominent loyalists, points to a sectarian abduction which ended with the brutal murder of this young lad."
Loyalists, mirror-opposites of the IRA, are supposed to be observing an October 1994 ceasefire.
But a breakaway group called the Loyalist Volunteer Force has said it will keep fighting what it sees as the IRA's threat to Northern Ireland's British status.
